This seems rather wasteful to allocate new arrays over and over just to use as arguments.

Wouldn't `TextDecoder.decode` automatically make sure we use the fastest possible implementation?

Good call — switched to a module-level `TextDecoder('latin1')` singleton in 489ba74. Uses the engine's native implementation, eliminates both the chunk-loop allocations and the explicit subarray calls.

I went with `'latin1'` (Windows-1252 in WHATWG encoding spec) rather than the default UTF-8 to keep the mapping bijective — UTF-8 would produce replacement characters (U+FFFD) for byte sequences that aren't valid UTF-8, which could cause distinct binary values to compare equal. Windows-1252 maps every byte value 0–255 to a unique code point, so the comparable-string guarantee holds for taint tracking.

The test makes it impossible to check if the leak is in React because the app code is leaking the signal itself. What is the real-world scenario that reproduces a memory leak? Is that still happening on the latest version on `main`?

Thanks — this is a fair concern. I think there are two separate things to distinguish here: what the React regression test is proving, and what the end-to-end reproduction is proving.

The test in this PR is intentionally a narrow regression test for the React invariant: the completion `cacheSignal()` abort reason should not capture a stack. It goes through the Flight completion path and verifies that the actual reason stored on `signal.reason` has no stack frames. It is not intended to be the leak reproducer by itself.

The real-world reproduction is the one from vercel/next.js#84648. The workload does not retain the `cacheSignal` from application code; it uses a dynamic server component with a slow upstream and clients disconnecting while the render is in progress. Under sustained high concurrency, retained heap grows after forced GC. The same workload was independently reproduced on Next 16.3.1 / 16.2.12 with React 19.2.8 and Node 24.

The strongest evidence there is the A/B with `--stack-trace-limit=0`: without the flag, retained heap after the load rounds was 407–2264 MB; with it, 68–157 MB. The two sets did not overlap, and the `stackTraceLimit=0` arm showed no accumulating trend across rounds. This is what led me to the React `new Error()` / captured CallSites retention path rather than application-level retention.

I also agree that suppressing the stack globally does not isolate this exact React call site, since it affects other stack-producing paths as well. That is why I'm treating the A/B as evidence that captured stacks are the dominant retained cost on this client-abort path, rather than as a proof that only this single `new Error()` is responsible.

For the second question, the issue is still reproducible on currently published React/Next versions; #84648 contains the recent independent reproductions. I can also run the shared repro against current React `main` to make that comparison explicit.

The breaks intentional behavior explained in https://github.com/react/react/pull/37037. Unfortunately, we didn't have a test. #37037 should highlight that this needs a different fix/feature consideration than just cutting the chain.

@eps1lon You're right  my previous change that severs previous/awaited directly in the destroy hook breaks the intentional behavior the new test validates. The strong reference chain is deliberately kept so that I/O nodes remain reachable for debug info emission even after intermediate Promises are garbage-collected.

We could then just model the render as having a lifetime and we always abort the renderlifetime controller when the render completes. functionaly it's the same thing though so maybe not worth it?
Nice idea, that made the cleanup much simpler. It also automatically handles the cancelled stream case.

How fast is this transition? Did you try it out on some large profile traces, where the search might take a while?

Would it make sense to display some loading indicator? Gated with this:
```
const searchIsPending = searchText !== deferredSearchText;
```

Added `searchIsPending` (`searchText !== deferredSearchText`) and wired it up to show a spinner in the search input while matching is in progress. I also benchmarked the matching logic on synthetic trees: it takes around **2.5ms** for **60k fibers** and about **5ms** for **100k fibers**, so the search itself stays well within a frame budget. I also profiled a synthetic commit with roughly **60k fibers**—the spinner appears as expected, and any remaining delay comes from re-rendering the flamegraph. Switching commits without searching is just as slow, so that overhead already existed and only shows up with unrealistically large commits.

This change should have broken something in ReactFlightServer. Suggests that we have some untested serialization path with large string serialization.

Even if the rationale was true though we can't land this change because the layering implies you get back an accurate byteLength. We'd have to rename to getApproximateByteLength etc...

Unless this is like the entirety of the perf win it doesn't seem worth the effort to rewrite the parts that use this length for approximating heuristics so let's just drop it.

If you want to see what would be broken by this check out `emitTextChunk` in ReactFlightServer
I don't think this check is an optimization tbh. it's checked in `parseModelString` and will just return the value there.

The check is duplicated, but the point is avoiding the function call. `parseModelString` is a large function with many switch cases, so neither GCC nor V8 will inline it. Without the guard, every non-`$` string (class names, text content, attribute values, etc.) pays for argument setup, stack frame push/pop, the same `value[0] === '$'` check inside, and return. With the guard, those strings never enter the function. I haven't measured the impact though, so it would be good to verify with your benchmarks.

We should try to avoid recursion when not necessary. For example, a pattern we typically use is check if something is resolved first and then initialize and then check if something is initialized instead of a single switch.

In this case, there can also be a lot of listeners when there's a lot of references to the same thing so in theory you can actually stack overflow because of this recursion.

Instead, you should check if the status has changed to initialized or errored here and if so call `wakeChunk` or `rejectChunk` respectively.
We shouldn't create the closure outside the condition. Maybe it's optimized but we should make sure.
But it's used in both branches of the condition.
In that case you should move it out to a reusable function in module scope and then call that from the closure. So that the closure only needs to be allocated in the delayed branch.
Then `addDebugInfo` can be hoisted out.
Ideally we'd check if `!suspendedBySet.delete(instance)` first before doing the loop so that in the common case when we do succeed in deleting it, there's no reason to check.
